meta.title: Reading a shophouse façade | Five Foot Way Journal
meta.description: How to date a Singapore shophouse from its front: the six styles, from early plain fronts to Art Deco, and what the tiles, shutters and five-foot way tell you.

title: Reading a shophouse façade
excerpt: Six styles in a hundred years, and how to tell them apart from the pavement.

body.p: A shophouse is a simple idea: a narrow building, two or three storeys high, with a shop or workshop on the ground floor and the family living above. Thousands were built in Singapore between the 1840s and the 1960s, terraced side by side, each with its covered walkway in front. The plan barely changed. The fronts did, and once you know what to look for, you can date a street from across the road.

The oldest surviving shophouses, from the mid-19th century, are low and plain: two storeys, one or two small windows above, very little decoration. You will find them in parts of Chinatown and along the river. Their simplicity is the clue.

body.h2: The first transitional and late styles

body.p: Towards the end of the century, shophouses rose to three storeys and gained more windows, often with timber shutters and fanlights above. Then, in the decades around 1900, decoration arrived in force: plaster garlands, Chinese motifs, pilasters and, above all, glazed tiles. This late style is the one most people picture, and Joo Chiat and Koon Seng Road are full of it.

The bright tiles that frame doors and windows were mostly made in England, Belgium and later Japan, and shipped east as a fashionable, washable decoration. Peranakan families loved them. Look for floral motifs, peacocks and fruit. Today, many old tiles are rescued when buildings are restored and sold again in specialist shops.

By the 1930s, taste had changed. Façades became flatter, with geometric patterns, vertical fins, and the year of construction moulded into the parapet. After the war, the last shophouses were plainer still, with horizontal concrete sun shades and no ornament at all.

body.h2: What to look for on your walk

ul: **Count the windows** on the upper floor: one or two suggests an early building, three a later one.
**Look up at the parapet** for a date or a family name.
**Check the pintu pagar**, the waist-high swing doors in front of the main door in residential terraces.
**Notice the five-foot way's floor**: original encaustic tiles survive in a few places. Watch your step, as levels change from one house to the next.

body.p: The best streets to practise on are Keong Saik Road and Club Street in Chinatown, Joo Chiat Road and Koon Seng Road in Katong, and Emerald Hill near Orchard. Walk them early, when the low sun brings out the relief on the plaster.
